The relationship between Master Task Cards and Part Numbers is fundamental to Maximo for Aviation's automated maintenance generation and statusing capability. Part Number Linkage​ Master Task Cards are linked to configuration-managed (CM) part numbers through the Part Numbers tab. This relationship enables: Automatic Task Card Generation - When an asset with a linked part number is validated by BDI, Task Cards are automatically created Component Tracking - Tasks follow components through their lifecycle (installation, removal, shop visit) Configuration Control - Ensures correct tasks are applied based on installed components Maintenance Planning - Links maintenance requirements to specific components Part Number Table Fields: Field Description Part Number CM part number from Part Number Master Description Part description Vendor Part manufacturer or vendor Description Additional description or notes The Part Number relationship is what enables "configuration-aware" maintenance the system automatically knows what maintenance is required based on what components are installed on each aircraft. Multiple Part Numbers: A single Master Task Card can be linked to multiple part numbers Useful for tasks that apply to different variants or alternates All linked part numbers will trigger Task Card generation Enables fleet commonality and standardization

Frequency configuration is one of the most critical aspects of Master Task Cards, defining when maintenance tasks become due. Maximo for Aviation supports multiple frequency definition methods to accommodate various maintenance philosophies. Frequency Definition Methods​ Master Task Cards support three primary methods for defining when tasks are due: Intervals and Thresholds - Traditional fixed-interval maintenance Time-Based Iterations - Sequential calendar-based task progression Meter-Based Iterations - Sequential usage-based task progression Special Frequency Information​ Refer to the Maintenance Task Library topic for an explanation of the fields within this section. Life Span: Start Date - When task becomes active Stop Date - When task is no longer required. The BDI will automatically de-activate the associated Task Cards once the date is exceeded. Alert and Warning Interval State: Defines when alert and warnings are issued before task becomes due: Option Description Example Absolute from Active Fixed time from task activation / last completion 30 days after activation Percent of Frequency from Active Percentage of interval from activation 80% of interval after activation Absolute prior to Due Fixed time before due date / count 500 FH before due Work Order Generation Information: Field Description Use Last Work Order's Start Information to Calculate Next Due Frequency? Determines if the task is treated as a Fixed or Floating. Fixed tasks are next due based on the prior work orders target start date. Floating Tasks are based on when the previous work order was completed (Actual Finish Date). Extended Date Date to which task can be extended Update Existing Task Cards? Update all existing Task Cards when Master Task Card changes Adjust Next Due Date? Adjust next due date for existing Task Cards

The Intervals and Thresholds method defines fixed-interval maintenance where tasks become due at regular intervals based on calendar time or meter readings. Standard Intervals​ Standard Intervals define when the task becomes due: Interval Definition: Field Description Example Frequency Type CALENDAR or METER CALENDAR, METER Frequency Numeric interval value 5.00, 5000.00 Frequency Units Unit of measure YEARS, OHAPU (APU Hours) Apply Adjustment Factor? Apply adjustment calculation Checked/Unchecked Interval Details: When you expand an interval, additional configuration options appear: Field Description Alert and Warning Frequency Units Unit for alert/warning calculations Alert Interval How far in advance to alert ("EBA" BDI Problem Code is reported as part of the aircraft configuration status) Warning Interval How far in advance to warn ("EBW" BDI Problem Code is reported as part of the aircraft configuration status) Tolerance Units Unit for tolerance Higher Tolerance Allowable extension beyond due Lower Tolerance Allowable early completion The Alert Interval in combination with the Alert and Warning Interval State determines when the BDI will automatically generate a Work Order from the related Task Card. Calendar Frequency Examples: Frequency Units Description 5.00 YEARS Every 5 years 24.00 MONTHS Every 24 months (2 years) 90.00 DAYS Every 90 days 1.00 DAYS Daily Meter Frequency Examples: Frequency Units Description 5,000.00 OHAPU Every 5,000 APU operating hours 12,000.00 FH Every 12,000 flight hours 10,000.00 FC Every 10,000 flight cycles 20,000.00 EH Every 20,000 engine hours Example Configuration: Task: APU Overhaul Frequency Type: CALENDAR Frequency: 5.00 YEARS Alert Interval: 14.00 DAYS (alert 14 days before due) Warning Interval: 7.00 DAYS (warn 7 days before due) Higher Tolerance: (no extension allowed) Lower Tolerance: (no early completion allowed) Standard Thresholds​ Standard Thresholds define when the first or initial instance of the maintenance task is due. This is distinct from Standard Intervals, which determine the frequency of all subsequent occurrences after the initial task is completed. Threshold vs. Interval: Component Purpose Example Threshold Defines when the FIRST occurrence is due First inspection due at 1,000 FH after installation Interval Defines when SUBSEQUENT occurrences are due Repeat every 5,000 FH after first inspection Threshold Configuration: Thresholds use the same structure as intervals but represent the initial due point: Field Description Frequency Type CALENDAR or METER Frequency Initial threshold value Frequency Units Unit of measure Apply Adjustment Factor? Apply adjustment calculation Threshold Examples: Frequency Units Purpose 1,000.00 FH First inspection due at 1,000 flight hours 90.00 DAYS First check due 90 days after installation 500.00 FC First inspection due at 500 cycles How Thresholds and Intervals Work Together: Example: Engine Borescope Inspection Threshold: 1,000.00 FH (First inspection) Interval: 5,000.00 FH (Recurring inspections) Timeline: 0 FH: Engine installed 1,000 FH: First borescope inspection due (THRESHOLD) 6,000 FH: Second borescope inspection due (1,000 + 5,000 INTERVAL) 11,000 FH: Third borescope inspection due (6,000 + 5,000 INTERVAL) 16,000 FH: Fourth borescope inspection due (11,000 + 5,000 INTERVAL) Thresholds are particularly useful for break-in inspections, initial service checks, or any maintenance that has a different first-time interval compared to recurring intervals. Multiple Intervals and Thresholds: A Master Task Card can have multiple intervals and thresholds: Multiple Intervals - Task becomes due when ANY interval is reached (whichever occurs first) Multiple Thresholds - Multiple warning points for different planning horizons Combined - Mix of calendar and meter-based intervals Example: Combined Frequency Task: C-Check Inspection Interval 1: 12,000.00 FH (flight hours) Interval 2: 72.00 MONTHS (calendar) Threshold 1: 500.00 FH (warn at 11,500 FH) Threshold 2: 14.00 DAYS (warn 14 days before calendar due) Result: Task becomes due at 12,000 FH OR 72 months, whichever occurs first Warnings issued at appropriate thresholds for each frequency type

Time-Based Iterations provide a sequential, calendar-based approach to maintenance where tasks progress through a defined sequence of intervals. This method is ideal for progressive inspections, calibrations, or maintenance programs that require different actions at different intervals. Time-Based Iteration Concept​ Instead of a single repeating interval, Time-Based Iterations define a sequence of calendar-based frequencies. Each iteration can have: Different interval lengths Different job cards Different alert and warning intervals Sequential progression through the iteration cycle Key Features: Sequential Progression - Task moves from iteration 1 to 2 to 3, etc. Variable Intervals - Each iteration can have a different frequency Iteration-Specific Job Cards - Different work instructions for each iteration Loop Capability - Option to return to first iteration after completing the sequence Configuring Time-Based Iterations​ Iteration Table Fields: Field Description Frequency Calendar interval value Frequency units MONTHS, DAYS, YEARS Alert and Warning Frequency Units Unit for alerts/warnings Alert interval Advance alert time Warning interval Advance warning time Iterations of this frequency Number of times this iteration occurs Iteration sequence number Position in the sequence Job Card Specific job card for this iteration Time-Based Iteration Examples​ Example 1: Progressive Calibration Program Equipment: Precision Test Equipment Requirement: Calibration intervals that increase with equipment maturity Iteration 1: - Frequency: 6 MONTHS - Iterations: 2 (occurs twice) - Sequence: 1 - Job Card: JPCAL101 (Initial Calibration) Iteration 2: - Frequency: 12 MONTHS - Iterations: 2 (occurs twice) - Sequence: 2 - Job Card: JPCAL102 (Standard Calibration) Iteration 3: - Frequency: 24 MONTHS - Iterations: 1 (occurs once) - Sequence: 3 - Job Card: JPCAL103 (Extended Calibration) Progression: Month 0: Equipment becomes operational Month 6: Iteration 1, Occurrence 1 (JPCAL101) Month 12: Iteration 1, Occurrence 2 (JPCAL101) Month 24: Iteration 2, Occurrence 1 (JPCAL102) Month 36: Iteration 2, Occurrence 2 (JPCAL102) Month 60: Iteration 3, Occurrence 1 (JPCAL103) Month 84: [Depends on Loop Iterations setting] Example 2: Phased Inspection Program Task: Structural Inspection Program Requirement: Different inspection depths at different intervals Iteration 1: - Frequency: 24 MONTHS - Iterations: 1 - Sequence: 1 - Job Card: JPBI001 (Basic Inspection) Iteration 2: - Frequency: 12 MONTHS - Iterations: 1 - Sequence: 2 - Job Card: JPDI001 ( Detailed Inspection) Progression: Month 0: New component installed Month 24: Iteration 1 (Basic Inspection) Month 36: Iteration 2 (Detailed Inspection) Month 48: [Depends on Loop Iterations setting] Loop Iterations Checkbox​ The Loop Iterations checkbox controls what happens after the final iteration in the sequence is completed: Loop Iterations = Checked (Enabled): After completing the final iteration, the task returns to Iteration 1 The cycle repeats indefinitely Useful for ongoing maintenance programs Example: Calibration program that cycles through inspection depths Loop Iterations = Unchecked (Disabled): After completing the final iteration, the task stops and the Task Card is made inactive No further work orders are generated Useful for one-time progressive programs Example: Break-in inspection program for new equipment The Loop Iterations setting is critical for determining whether your maintenance program is cyclical (repeating) or finite (one-time). Choose based on your maintenance philosophy and regulatory requirements. If the "Iterations of this Frequency" field is left empty for the last iteration in the sequence then the associated task card will continue indefinitely at the last iteration frequency.

Meter-Based Iterations provide a sequential, usage-based approach to maintenance where tasks progress through a defined sequence of meter intervals. It operates in an almost identical manner to the time based iterations. This method is ideal for progressive inspections based on operating hours, cycles, or other usage metrics. Meter-Based Iteration Concept​ Similar to Time-Based Iterations, but driven by meter readings rather than calendar time. Each iteration can have: Different meter interval lengths Different job cards Different alert and warning thresholds Sequential progression through the iteration cycle Variable iterations (different number of occurrences per iteration) Configuring Meter-Based Iterations​ Step 1: Select Meter First, define which meter drives the iterations: Field Description Meter Meter code (FH, FC, EH, etc.) Description Meter description Step 2: Configure Iteration Flags Field Description Variable Iterations? Allow different iteration counts per frequency Loop Iterations? Return to first iteration after completing sequence Step 3: Define Frequency Iterations For each iteration in the sequence: Field Description Frequency Meter interval value Alert interval Advance alert threshold Warning interval Advance warning threshold Iterations of this frequency How many times this iteration occurs Iteration sequence number Position in the sequence Job card Specific job card for this iteration Meter-Based Iteration Examples​ Example 1: Engine Borescope Inspection Program Component: Turbine Engine Meter: EH (Engine Hours) Requirement: Progressive borescope inspections with increasing intervals Variable Iterations: Checked Loop Iterations: Checked Iteration 1: - Frequency: 600.00 EH - Alert interval: 50.00 EH - Warning interval: 25.00 EH - Iterations: 1 - Sequence: 2 - Job Card: JPBORO001 (Initial Borescope) Iteration 2: - Frequency: 1,200.00 EH - Alert interval: 50.00 EH - Warning interval: 25.00 EH - Iterations: 1 - Sequence: 1 - Job Card: JPBORO002 (Standard Borescope) Progression: 0 EH: Engine installed 600 EH: Iteration 2, Occurrence 1 (Initial Borescope - JPBORO001) 1,800 EH: Iteration 1, Occurrence 1 (Standard Borescope - JPBORO002) 3,000 EH: Iteration 2, Occurrence 1 (Initial Borescope - JPBORO001) [Loop back] 3,600 EH: Iteration 1, Occurrence 1 (Standard Borescope - JPBORO002) ...continues cycling Meter-Based Iterations with Variable Iterations and Loop Iterations provide maximum flexibility for complex maintenance programs that need to adapt to component usage patterns and maturity.

Master Task Card Actions provide powerful automation capabilities that allow one task (the "primary" task) to trigger actions on other related tasks (the "secondary" tasks). This feature enables sophisticated maintenance logic and workflow automation. Actions Concept and Purpose​ What Are Master Task Card Actions? Master Task Card Actions define automated responses that occur when specific events happen with a primary task. These actions affect secondary tasks on the same asset, enabling: Coordinated Maintenance - Link related tasks so they work together Workflow Automation - Automatically activate, deactivate, or complete related tasks Maintenance Logic - Implement complex maintenance rules and dependencies Event-Driven Maintenance - Trigger tasks based on component installation/removal Master Task Card Actions are limited to primary and secondary Task Cards for the same CM Item or configuration-managed asset. Actions cannot affect Task Cards on different assets. Action Configuration​ Action Table Fields: Field Description Action Type Type of action to perform Secondary Master Task Card Target Master Task Card for the action Description Description of the secondary task Reset Job Card Sequence? Whether to reset job card sequence Scenario When the action is triggered Action Details: When you expand an action: Field Description Action Type Type of action to perform Description Scenario description Secondary Master Task Card Target Master Task Card Reset Job Card Sequence? Reset job card sequence flag Activation Delay Unit Unit for activation delay Activation Delay Period Delay period value Action Types and Triggers​ Master Task Card Actions support multiple action types, each triggered by specific events: Work Order Completion Actions: These actions are triggered when a work order generated from the primary Task Card is completed: Action Type Effect Use Case ACTIVATE Changes secondary Task Card status to ACTIVE Enable a task after another task is completed. Example: Activate operational checks after installation task is complete. COMPLETE Marks secondary Task Card as complete and resets next due date Claim completion of a related task when primary task is done. Example: Complete follow-up inspection when main inspection is complete. CREATE WO Generates a work order from the secondary Task Card Automatically create work for a related task. Example: Generate calibration work order after equipment installation. DEACTIVATE Changes secondary Task Card status to INACTIVE Disable a task after another task is completed. Example: Deactivate temporary inspection after permanent fix is complete. Component Installation Actions: These actions are triggered when the asset associated with the primary Task Card is installed into a parent assembly: Action Type Effect Use Case ON-ACTIVATE Changes secondary Task Card status to ACTIVE when component is installed Enable tasks when component is installed. Example: Activate operational checks when engine is installed on aircraft. ON-DEACTIVATE Changes secondary Task Card status to INACTIVE when component is installed Disable tasks when component is installed. Example: Deactivate storeroom maintenance tasks when component goes on-wing. Component Removal Actions: These actions are triggered when the asset associated with the primary Task Card is removed from a parent assembly: Action Type Effect Use Case OFF-ACTIVATE Changes secondary Task Card status to ACTIVE when component is removed Enable tasks when component is removed. Example: Activate shop inspection when engine is removed from aircraft. OFF-DEACTIVATE Changes secondary Task Card status to INACTIVE when component is removed Disable tasks when component is removed. Example: Deactivate on-wing tasks when component is removed. Reset Job Card Sequence​ The Reset Job Card Sequence checkbox controls whether the job card sequence for the secondary Task Card is reset when the action is triggered: Reset Job Card Sequence = Checked: Job card sequence is reset to the beginning Useful when you want to restart a job card progression Example: After overhaul, reset calibration job card sequence to start from first calibration Reset Job Card Sequence = Unchecked: Job card sequence continues from current position Useful when you want to maintain progression Example: Continue with next job card in sequence after completing related task Activation Delay​ Actions can be configured with a delay before they take effect: Field Description Activation Delay Unit Unit for delay (DAYS, HOURS, etc.) Activation Delay Period Numeric delay value Use Cases for Activation Delay: Allow time for post-maintenance stabilization Coordinate with operational schedules Implement mandatory waiting periods Stagger related maintenance activities Master Task Card Actions provide powerful automation but should be carefully designed and tested. Incorrect action configuration can lead to unexpected Task Card status changes or maintenance gaps.

Maximo for Aviation introduces enhanced status management and revision control for Master Task Cards, providing better change tracking and configuration control. Status Management​ Status Field: Master Task Cards have a status field (MASTERPM.PLUSASTATUS) that controls their lifecycle: Status Description Task Card Generation DRAFT Master Task Card is being developed No Task Cards generated ACTIVE Master Task Card is approved and operational Task Cards generated automatically INACTIVE Master Task Card is no longer in use No new Task Cards generated. Existing Task Cards are deactivated PNDREV Pending revision (revision in progress) Changes are not put into effect into the new revision is activated REVISED Previous revision (superseded) Historical reference only Status Workflow: Create - New Master Task Card created with DRAFT status Configure - Set up frequencies, part numbers, actions, etc. Activate - Change status to ACTIVE when ready for use Revise - Create revision (status becomes PNDREV for new revision) Supersede - Previous revision changes to REVISED status Task Cards cannot be created from Master Task Cards unless they are in ACTIVE status. This ensures only approved, validated tasks are used for maintenance generation. Revision Control​ Revision Benefits: Full change tracking (what changed, when, by whom) Audit trail for regulatory compliance Controlled change management process Prevents accidental modifications to active tasks Maintains historical record of all revisions Updating Associated Task Cards: Revising Master Task Cards in OMPs​ Master Task Cards that are part of an Operators Maintenance Program (OMP) have special revision requirements. The revision creation process and activation of the new revision must be performed within the OMP application itself, not directly in the Master Task Cards application. OMP-Based Revision Process: When a Master Task Card is included in an OMP: Navigate to OMP Application - Open the OMP that contains the Master Task Card Locate Task - Find the Master Task Card in the OMP Tasks list Initiate Revision - Use the OMP's revision action for the task Make Changes - Applink to the Master Task Card to make modificiations to it and save. Return to the OMP once changes are made Activate Revision - Activate the new master task card revision using the change status icon on the OMP Task row within the OMP Propagate Changes - The system automatically triggers the update to the associated Task Cards by triggering BDI validation for the affected Aircraft. Be aware that the update of associated Task Cards is not immediate. The time taken for changes to be propagated depends on a numnber of factors including: number of aircraft and how the BDI and asynchronous job crontasks are configured. When a Master Task Card revision is activated: Automatic Update - BDI updates Task Cards during next asset validation Manual Update - Use "Update Associated Task Cards?" action for immediate update

The Extendable checkbox on a Master Task Card indicates that associated Task Cards can have their due dates or due counts extended through a controlled process. Extendable Checkbox: When checked, Task Cards generated from this Master Task Card can be extended Extensions are created through Task Card Extension records Extensions can be subject to approval workflow Provides controlled flexibility for operational needs Task Card Extension Process: Identify Need - Task Card approaching due date but cannot be completed Create Extension - Create Task Card Extension record Justify Extension - Document reason and new due date/count Approval - Submit for approval (if workflow configured) Apply Extension - Extension updates Task Card due date/count Track Extension - Extension history maintained for audit Use Cases for Extensions: Aircraft grounded for unrelated issues Parts availability delays Operational schedule conflicts Weather or facility constraints Regulatory approval for extension Task Card extensions must comply with regulatory requirements and manufacturer limitations. Some tasks (especially CMR tasks) may not be extendable or may require regulatory approval.

The Master Task Card application includes several additional tabs for comprehensive task documentation: Planning Tab​ Contains Master Task Card Actions (covered in detail above) and planning information: Master Task Card Actions configuration Planning notes and considerations Resource requirements Scheduling preferences Job Cards Tab​ Links detailed work instructions to the Master Task Card: Associates Job Cards with the task Job Cards define detailed work procedures and steps and resources required to peform the task (see separate guide on Job Card usage) OMP Tab​ Shows which Operators Maintenance Program includes this Master Task Card: Lists OMPs that reference this task Shows task applicability within each OMP Checks Tab​ Defines which maintenance checks include this task: Associates task with check-based maintenance Supports A-Check, C-Check, etc. organization Enables check-based work packaging Related Documents Tab​ Links supporting documentation to the Master Task Card: Technical manuals Service bulletins Engineering orders Illustrated parts catalogs Training materials Safety documentation Related Documentation: Maintenance Task Library (MTL) Operators Maintenance Program (OMP) Part Number Master Task Cards Application Build Data Interpreter (BDI)

The Maintenance Task Library (MTL) application enables organizations to import, manage, and validate maintenance task data from aircraft manufacturers' Maintenance Planning Documents (MPD). The MTL serves as an intermediate staging area where maintenance tasks are imported, reviewed, validated, and then converted into Master Task Cards as part of the Operators Maintenance Program (OMP) definition. Purpose and Workflow: The MTL application facilitates a structured workflow for managing manufacturer maintenance requirements: Import - Load maintenance task data from manufacturer MPD files (Excel format) Review - Examine imported tasks for completeness and accuracy Validate - Change status to VALID once tasks are verified Convert - Create Master Task Cards within the OMP from validated MTL tasks The MTL application acts as a bridge between manufacturer maintenance requirements and your organization's operational maintenance program, ensuring that all regulatory and manufacturer-mandated tasks are properly captured and implemented. Key Capabilities: Import maintenance tasks from manufacturer MPD files in Excel format Comprehensive task data including frequencies, intervals, and thresholds Task modification tracking (new, revised, deleted tasks) Validation workflow with status management Bulk conversion to Master Task Cards Integration with OMP application Support for multiple task types (inspections, services, overhauls, etc.) ATA chapter organization Skill and trade assignment Phase and zone information Part number associations Integration Points: Master Task Cards - Target for converted MTL tasks OMP Application - Provides an action for the bulk creation of Master Task Cards from the MTL record. Part Number Master - Links tasks to specific components Job Cards - Master Task Cards can be linked to existing active Job Cards or a "default" Job Card can be created for each MTL Task using Zone and Craft information. Benefits: Streamlines incorporation of manufacturer maintenance requirements Ensures compliance with regulatory and manufacturer mandates Reduces manual data entry and associated errors Maintains traceability from MPD to operational tasks Supports multiple MPD revisions and change tracking Enables efficient updates when manufacturers issue new MPD revisions

An MTL record represents a complete maintenance task library for a specific aircraft type and MPD revision. Header Information​ The MTL header contains identifying information and metadata about the task library: Field Description Example Required MTL Unique identifier for the MTL record A350 MPD Yes Description Descriptive name for the MTL record. A350 MPD Yes Status Current status of the MTL record VALID, DRAFT, REVIEW Yes Revision MPD revision number 0, 1, 2 Yes Revision Date Date of the MPD revision 30/10/2025 Yes Aircraft Manufacturer Manufacturer of the aircraft AIRBUS, BOEING Yes Organization Operating organization EAGLE Yes Comments Additional notes or comments Free text No Status Values: Status Description Usage DRAFT MTL is being created or edited Initial import and review phase VALID MTL has been validated and approved Ready for Master Task Card creation within the OMP INACTIVE MTL has been replaced by newer revision or is no longer required Historical reference only Only MTL records with VALID status can be used to create Master Task Cards. Ensure thorough review and validation before changing status to VALID. Revision Management: Each MPD revision should be imported as a new MTL record or revision Revision numbers typically follow manufacturer's MPD revision scheme Revision dates track when the manufacturer issued the MPD Multiple revisions can coexist in the system for historical reference Previous revisions can be retained for audit and traceability MTL Tasks​ The MTL Tasks section contains the detailed maintenance task information imported from the manufacturer's MPD. This is the core content of the MTL record. Task Information Fields: Field Description Example Modification Type Indicates if task is new, revised, or deleted N (New), R (Revised), D (Deleted) or blank (Unchanged) Task Number Manufacturer's task number 251000-00M06-01 Task Code Short code for task type OPC, DET, DIS, GVI Description Detailed task description COCKPIT, PASSENGER COMPARTMENT SEATS ATA Chapter ATA chapter code 25-00 (Equipment/Furnishings) Skill Required maintenance skill/trade AF (Airframe) Phase Maintenance phase or check A, B, C, D Deferral? Whether task can be deferred Checked/Unchecked Out of Phase? Indicates whether the task is typically done "out of phase". Outside of a larger inspection event (A Check etc) Checked/Unchecked Hour Interval Flight hour interval 12000 FH Cycle Interval Flight cycle interval 600 FC Calendar Interval Calendar time interval 72.00 MO Calendar Unit Unit for calendar interval MONTHS, DAYS, YEARS Task Code Examples: Code Description Typical Usage OPC Operational Check Functional verification DET Detailed Inspection Thorough visual inspection DIS Discard Time-change item replacement GVI General Visual Inspection Basic visual check SVC Service Lubrication, replenishment RST Restoration Overhaul, major repair FNC Functional Check System operation verification Modification Type Indicators: R - Revised task (changes from previous MPD revision) Blank - Unchanged task (same as previous revision) D - Deleted task (removed in this revision) N - New task (added in this revision) ATA Chapter Organization: Tasks are organized by ATA chapter codes which represent aircraft systems. ATA Codes are defined within the "Component Codes" application.

The "Import File" action is the primary method for loading maintenance task data from manufacturer MPD files into the MTL application. This process automates the creation of MTL tasks from structured Excel files. Import Process Overview​ Prerequisites: Manufacturer MPD file in Excel format (.xls or .xlsx) File must follow the MTL import file format specification Import Workflow: Prepare Import File Obtain manufacturer MPD file Verify file format matches MTL import specification Review data for completeness Initiate Import Navigate to MTL application Open existing MTL record or create new one Enter MTL header information / required fields and save. Click Import MTL action Upload File Select Excel file from local system and confirm Upload begins automatically and processing begins. Monitor Processing System processes each row in the file The "Refresh" button can be used to refresh the progress. Errors are captured and reported Review Results Check total lines processed Review any errors encountered. The error gives details of the row and column within the uploaded file which were invalid. Verify task data was imported correctly Import File Format​ The MTL import file must be an Excel spreadsheet with specific columns that map to MTL task fields. The file format is defined in the MTL Import File Format.xls template. Download MTL Import File Format Template Required Columns: The import file must be structured so that the columns match the order as those defined in the MTL File Format spreadsheet. Import File Example​ An example import file is provided based on the Airbus A350 Maintenance Planning Document: Download A350 MPD Import Example Example File Contents: The A350 example file demonstrates: Proper column structure and naming Task numbering conventions ATA chapter organization Multiple task types (OPC, DET, DIS) Frequency definitions (hours, cycles, calendar) Modification type indicators Skill assignments Phase associations Ensure that the Excel file does not contain any merged cells, hidden rows, or complex formatting that might interfere with the import process. Use simple, flat table structure. Import Validation and Error Handling​ During the import process, the system performs validation on each row: Validation Checks: Required fields are populated Data types are correct (numeric fields contain numbers) Task codes are valid ATA chapters follow standard format Intervals are positive numbers Calendar units are recognized values Error Reporting: The Import MTL dialog displays detailed error information: Field Description Total Lines Total number of rows in the file Lines Processed Number of rows successfully processed Errors Number of rows with errors Status Overall import status (COMPLETE, ERROR, IN PROGRESS) Error Details Table: For each error encountered, the system provides: Line - Row number in the Excel file Column Num - Column number where error occurred Card - Task number or identifier Error - Description of the error Common Import Errors: Error Cause Resolution Required field missing Task number or code not provided Add missing data to Excel file Invalid data type Text in numeric field Correct data type in Excel file Invalid task code Unrecognized task code Use valid task code from list Duplicate task number Task number already exists Remove duplicate or update existing Invalid ATA chapter ATA code format incorrect Use standard ATA format (XX-XX) Invalid calendar unit Unrecognized unit Use DAYS, MONTHS, or YEARS If the import completes with 0 errors, all tasks were successfully imported and are ready for review. If errors are present, correct the Excel file and re-import. Post-Import Activities​ After successful import: Review Imported Tasks Navigate to MTL Tasks tab Verify task count matches expected number Spot-check task details for accuracy Review modification types (R, N, D) Validate Task Data Check frequency definitions Verify ATA chapter assignments Confirm skill assignments Review phase associations Handle Errors Export error report if needed Correct errors in source Excel file Re-import corrected file Verify error resolution Update MTL Status Change status from DRAFT to VALID when approved

Each MTL task can have one or more frequency definitions that specify when the maintenance task must be performed. Frequencies can be based on a meter such as flight hours or flight cycles, calendar time, or combinations thereof. Frequency Types​ Meter-Based Frequencies: Flight Hours (FH) - Based on accumulated flight time Flight Cycles (FC) - Based on takeoff/landing cycles Engine Hours (EH) - Based on engine operating time APU Hours (AH) - Based on APU operating time Calendar-Based Frequencies: Days - Calendar days elapsed Months - Calendar months elapsed Years - Calendar years elapsed Combined Frequencies: Tasks can have both meter and calendar frequencies Task becomes due when either threshold is reached (whichever occurs first) Common for critical inspections and time-change items Frequency Configuration Fields​ Special Frequency Information: Field Description Usage Due on Last Deadline? Task due on last applicable deadline Checked for critical tasks Soft Task? Task can be performed later than deadline without safety impacts Checked for flexible tasks Note? Task has special notes or instructions Checked when notes exist Fatigue Rating Fatigue sensitivity rating Numeric value Initialization Date Event that starts frequency counting Date of Manufacture NR? National Requirement Checked for tasks which have been indicated as required by a civil aviation authority VR? Vendor requirement Checked for tasks where the Vendor has indciated this is a mandatory task Sample Task? Task is a sample/statistical task Checked for sampling program tasks Alert and Warning Interval State: Defines when warnings are issued before task becomes due: Option Description Absolute from Active Fixed time after task becomes active (typically based on last completion date) Percent of Frequency from Active Percentage of interval Absolute prior to Due Fixed time before due Frequency Definition Table​ The Frequencies table shows all interval definitions for the task: Field Description Example Sample Frequency? Whether this is a sampling frequency Checked/Unchecked Type Frequency type INTERVAL, CALENDAR Frequency Type Meter or calendar basis METER, CALENDAR Frequency Interval value 12,000.00 Frequency Unit Unit of measure FH, FC, MONTHS Frequency Examples: Task Type Frequency Definition Description A-Check 500 FH or 90 Days Whichever occurs first C-Check 12,000 FH or 72 Months Major inspection Daily Inspection 1 Day Every calendar day Engine Overhaul 20,000 EH Time between overhauls Landing Gear 10,000 FC Based on cycles Life Limited Part 25,000 FH Mandatory replacement When multiple frequencies are defined for a task, the system tracks all of them and the task becomes due when any frequency threshold is reached. This ensures compliance with the most restrictive requirement. Threshold and Tolerance​ Threshold (Warning Point): Advance warning before task becomes due Allows time for planning and scheduling Typically 10-20% of the interval Example: 500 FH threshold for 5,000 FH interval Tolerance (Grace Period): Allowable extension beyond due point Provides scheduling flexibility Must comply with regulatory limits Example: +50 FH tolerance after due Initial vs. Recurring Intervals: Initial Interval - First interval after installation or overhaul Recurring Interval - Standard interval for subsequent occurrences Initial intervals often shorter to detect early issues

The MTL application provides several additional tabs for comprehensive task documentation: Part Numbers Tab​ Associates specific part numbers with the task: Links task to components that require the maintenance Supports multiple part numbers per task Enables part-specific task applicability Facilitates material planning If the Part Numbers for an MTL Tasks are not specified then the Master Task Card created from it within the OMP will be linked to the Aircraft Part Numbers (as defined within the Model). Use Cases: Component overhaul tasks Part-specific inspections Zones Tab​ Defines aircraft zones where the task is performed: Organizes tasks by physical location Supports access planning Enables zone-based work packaging Zone Examples: 100 - Nose section 200 - Forward fuselage 300 - Center fuselage 400 - Aft fuselage 500 - Wings 600 - Empennage Aircraft Zones are defined within the separate "Zones" application. Access Tab​ Documents access requirements for the task, such as: Panels that must be removed Doors that must be opened Special access equipment needed Access time estimates Access Information: Access panel numbers Opening /Closing and Total Access Time Crafts and Qualifications Tab​ Specifies required skills and qualifications: Maintenance trades required Certification requirements Special qualifications needed Training prerequisites Craft Examples: Airframe (AF) Avionics (AV) Electrical (EL) Powerplant (PP) Sheet Metal (SM) Each Craft must be associated with and Aircraft Zone where the work will take place. Related Documents Tab​ Links supporting documentation to the task: Technical manuals Service bulletins Engineering orders Work instructions Illustrated parts catalogs

Aircraft manufacturers periodically issue new revisions of their Maintenance Planning Documents. The MTL application supports managing multiple MPD revisions and tracking changes between revisions. Revision Management Strategy​ New MTL Record per Revision Create a new MTL record for each MPD revision Import new revision data using the Import File action New, revised, and deleted tasks should be specified within the file imported using the first column "Rev Code" Carefully review all tasks marked with modification type "R" (Revised) or "D" (Deleted) to understand the impact on your maintenance program and updating Master Task Cards. Related Documentation: Master Task Cards Application Operators Maintenance Program (OMP) Part Number Master Loading Data with MXLoader Additional Resources: MTL import file format specification MPD data mapping guidelines Frequency configuration best practices Revision management procedures Task code reference guide

The Operators Maintenance Program (OMP) application is a critical component of Maximo for Aviation that enables aircaft operators or maintainers to define, manage, and maintain their aircraft maintenance programs. An OMP represents the approved maintenance program and should define all required maintenance tasks, their frequencies, and applicability to specific aircraft in the fleet. The OMP application provides comprehensive functionality for: Creating and managing operator-specific maintenance programs Defining maintenance tasks and their intervals (calendar and meter-based) within the related Master Task Card application. Establishing aircraft effectivity and applicability rules Organizing tasks into maintenance checks Managing task frequencies and thresholds Tracking part number relationships and requirements Implementing complex effectivity logic including modification status The OMP serves as the master definition for all scheduled maintenance activities and integrates with Work Package planning, Master Task Cards, and aircraft configuration management. Key Capabilities: Multiple OMP versions for different aircraft models or configurations Flexible effectivity rules including serial number ranges and modification status Calendar and meter-based task intervals Check-based task grouping for efficient maintenance planning Advanced effectivity expressions using boolean logic Integration with Master Task Cards and Part Number Master Support for pre-modification and post-modification task applicability

Creation - Define new OMP with basic information and model association Effectivity Setup - Define which aircraft the OMP and tasks apply to Task Definition - Add Master Task Cards as OMP tasks. These are the individual maintenance tasks that are required . This often originates from the Maintenance Planning Document (MPD)) Check Organization - Group tasks into maintenance checks Submit for Approval - Status of the OMP is changed to SUBMIT prior to activation. Activation - Apply OMP to aircraft in the fleet (defined on the Effectivity tab) Maintenance - Update tasks, frequencies, and effectivity as needed using temporary revisions to individual tasks. Version Control - Manage OMP revisions and changes over time, eg if new MPD revisions are released. A well-structured OMP ensures regulatory compliance, optimizes maintenance scheduling, and provides a clear framework for all preventive maintenance activities. The OMP List page lists all OMP records together with revision and status. OMP records with a status of REVISED or INACTIVE are hidden by default.

The OMP Main Page displays key OMP information and serves as the navigation hub for detailed configuration. It also displays a list of the OMP Tasks (Master Task Cards) which are included as part of the maintenance program definition. Once the OMP is activated individual Task Cards will be created for each Aicraft covered by the OMP (depending on applicability). OMP Header Information: Field Description OMP Unique identifier for the maintenance program Revision Version or revision number of the OMP Description Description of the OMP purpose and scope Operator The operating organization that owns this maintenance program Status Current status (Active, Draft, Pending Revision or Submitted for Approval) Authority The authority responsible for approving maintenance organizations Approval Date Date when the OMP was approved and made active Expiration Date Date when the OMP expires (if applicable) Expiration Warning Date Date when the warning of pending OMP expiratin will be displayed (via BDI problem code)

Models - Aircraft models associated with this OMP Effectivity - Aircraft to which the OMP is applicable OMP Tasks - Master Task Cards included in the maintenance program Checks - Grouped collections of tasks for maintenance planning Creating a New OMP: Navigate to the OMP application Click New OMP or use the + button Enter a unique OMP Number Provide a descriptive name for the program Select the operator organization Select the authority organization Save the new OMP record Once saved, the OMP Number cannot be changed as it part of the primary key of the record. OMP Status Management: Draft - OMP is being developed and not yet active Submit - OMP has been submitted for approval. It becomes readonly at this stage. Active - OMP is currently in use and applied to aircraft. Temporary revisions can be made to individual tasks. Inactive - OMP is no longer active but retained for historical purposes Pending - OMP has been revised and this new revision can be modified. Best Practices: Use clear, descriptive OMP Numbers that indicate the aircraft type and version Document the purpose and scope in the description field Maintain version control through revision numbers Review and update OMPs regularly to reflect regulatory changes Coordinate OMP changes with maintenance planning and operations

The Models section defines which aircraft models are associated with the OMP. This relationship is fundamental as it determines which Master Task Cards can be added to the OMP and ensures that maintenance tasks are appropriate for the aircraft type. Model Association: Links the OMP to specific aircraft models in the system Determines which Master Task Cards are eligible for inclusion Supports multiple models within a single OMP (for fleet commonality) Enables model-specific task variations when needed Adding Models to an OMP: Navigate to the Models tab on the OMP Main Page Click Add Row to add a new model association Select the aircraft model from the lookup Save the model association Model Information: Field Description Model Aircraft model designation (e.g., 737-800, A320-200) Description Full description of the aircraft model The model relationship is used to filter Master Task Cards when adding OMP tasks. Only task cards related to the associated models will be available for selection. This relationship is established using the Part Numbers defined within the Aircraft Model or related sub models (via installation points). Model-Based Task Filtering: Master Task Cards must be related to the model through Part Number relationships Task cards must have the same "Operator" value as the OMP Task cards cannot be associated with another active OMP Multi-Model OMPs: When an OMP covers multiple aircraft models (common in fleets with similar aircraft): Define all applicable models in the Models section Use effectivity rules to specify which tasks apply to which models Leverage the MODEL() function in advanced effectivity expressions Consider model-specific task variations where necessary

The Effectivity section defines the list of aircraft to which the OMP is applicable. This is a critical component that determines which aircraft in the fleet are governed by this maintenance program. For active OMPs, the "Applied" checkbox indicates whether the OMP is currently active against each individual aircraft. Effectivity Management: Defines which specific aircraft are covered by the OMP Tracks whether the OMP is currently applied to each aircraft Indicates if an Aircraft has been designated a "Sample Aircraft". Sample Aircraft may have differing frequncies (Threshold or Interval) at the individual OMP Task level. Effectivity Fields: Field Description Aircraft Aircraft number (ASSETNUM) Tail Number Aicraft tail number/ registration MSN Manufacturer serial number (MSN) Model Aircraft Model Variant Aircraft Variant Date of Manufacture Date Date of Aircraft Manufacture Sample Aicraft Checkbox indicating if the Aircraft has been designated a sample aircraft Applied Checkbox indicating if OMP is currently active against the aircraft Adding Aircraft to OMP Effectivity: Navigate to the Effectivity tab on the OMP Main Page Click "Select Aicraft" button and then select one or more aicraft from the resulting dialog. Save the OMP record Only Aircraft with the same Model as listed on the OMP Models tab will be available for selection. Only Aircraft with the same Operator as the Operator on the OMP itself will be available for selection. Applying an OMP to Aircraft: When the "Applied" checkbox is checked: The OMP becomes the active maintenance program for that aircraft All OMP tasks are evaluated for applicability to the aircraft Preventive maintenance schedules are generated based on OMP tasks Work packages can be created using the OMP structure The aircraft's maintenance requirements are governed by this OMP Only one OMP can be applied to an aircraft at anyone time. Applying a new OMP typically supersedes the previous OMP and may require careful transition planning. For this reason if an Aircraft is added to an OMP after the OMP is activated it will not be automatically applied. Manual activation of the OMP can be performed using the BDI Status dialog in the Aircraft application. This is performed on the Alternative Configuration tab of the BDI Status dialog by selecting the OMP and clicking the "Apply Configuratation" button. Best Practices: Verify aircraft model matches OMP models before applying Document reasons for OMP changes in notes or comments Plan OMP transitions carefully to avoid maintenance gaps Coordinate with maintenance planning when applying new OMPs Review effectivity regularly to ensure accuracy

OMP Tasks are Master Task Cards that have been added to the Operators Maintenance Program. These tasks define the specific maintenance activities that must be performed on aircraft covered by the OMP. Master Task Cards must be related to the Model (via Part Number relationship) and have the same "Operator" value in order to be added to the OMP. Additionally, they cannot be associated with another active OMP. Master Task Card / OMP Tasks Characteristics: Include interval, threshold and other frequency information Define part number applicability at either the Airframe or Component Level Can be organized into maintenance checks OMP Tasks inherit their basic definition from Master Task Cards but include additional OMP-specific information such as frequency intervals, thresholds, and aircraft effectivity. Adding Tasks to an OMP: Navigate to the OMP Main tab Click Add OMP Task or Add Row Search for and select Master Task Cards that meet the criteria: Related to the OMP's associated models via Part Number relationship. Same operator value as the OMP Not already assigned to another active OMP Save the OMP 5 optionally set aircraft effectivity rules using either MSN or Modification Status applicability. OMP Task Information: Field Description Modification Type N, R, D Indicates if the Task is (N)ew, (R)evised or (D)eleted in the current OMP revision Task Number Task Number Description Task description from the Master Task Card Task Code Type of maintenance task (General Visual Inspection, Service, etc.) Revision The ATA Code to which the task relates Estimated Hours Labor hours required to complete the task Frequency Interval information (see Frequency section) Effectivity Aircraft applicability (see Effectivity section) Task Selection Criteria: The system enforces the following rules when adding tasks to an OMP: Model Relationship - Task must be related to one of the OMP's models through part number associations Operator Match - Task's operator field must match the OMP's operator Availability - Task cannot be assigned to another active OMP Status - Task must be in an active or approved status Using Master Task Cards as the foundation for OMP tasks ensures consistency across the maintenance program and enables centralized task management. Frequency​ The Frequency section defines interval and threshold information for each OMP task. Frequencies can be meter-based (flight hours, cycles, etc.) or calendar-based (days, months, years), and multiple frequency types can be specified for a single task. Frequency Types: Meter-Based - Driven by aircraft usage meters (hours, cycles, landings) Calendar-Based - Driven by elapsed time (days, months, years) Combined - Task due when either meter or calendar threshold is reached Whichever Occurs First - Most common approach for critical tasks Frequency Fields: Field Description Meter The meter type (Flight Hours, Cycles, Calendar Days, etc.) Interval The numeric interval value Frequency Combined interval and meter (e.g., "500 FH", "12 MO") Threshold Warning threshold before task becomes due Tolerance Allowable extension beyond due point Initial Interval First interval after aircraft delivery or modification Defining Task Frequency: Navigate to the Frequency tab within an OMP Task Click Add Row to add a frequency definition Select the meter type from the dropdown Enter the interval value Specify threshold (warning point before due) Define tolerance (allowable extension) Set initial interval if different from recurring interval Save the frequency definition Frequency Examples: Task Type Frequency Definition Description Daily Inspection 1 Calendar Day Performed every day A-Check 500 Flight Hours or 90 Days Whichever occurs first C-Check 5000 Flight Hours or 18 Months Major inspection interval Landing Gear 10000 Cycles Based on landing cycles Calendar Item 24 Months Every 2 years regardless of usage Threshold and Tolerance: Threshold - Advance warning point (e.g., 50 hours before due) Tolerance - Allowable extension (e.g., +10 hours after due) Used for maintenance planning and scheduling flexibility Helps optimize maintenance windows and resource utilization Tolerance values must comply with regulatory requirements and manufacturer recommendations. Exceeding tolerance may result in non-compliance. Initial vs. Recurring Intervals: Initial Interval - First interval after aircraft delivery, overhaul, or modification Recurring Interval - Standard interval for subsequent occurrences Initial intervals are often shorter to detect early issues System automatically switches to recurring interval after first completion Multiple Frequency Definitions: A single task can have multiple frequency definitions: Flight Hours AND Calendar Days (whichever occurs first) Different intervals for different aircraft configurations Escalating intervals based on aircraft age or usage Regional or operational variations Part Numbers​ The Part Numbers section lists all part numbers associated with the selected OMP Task or Master Task Card. This information is critical for: Identifying components affected by the maintenance task Ensuring correct parts are available for maintenance Tracking part number applicability and interchangeability Supporting material planning and procurement Part Number Information: Field Description Part Number Manufacturer part number Description Part description Manufacturer Part manufacturer Quantity Quantity required for the task Unit of Measure Unit (EA, SET, KIT, etc.) Consumable Whether part is consumed during task Alternate Parts List of acceptable alternate part numbers Part Number Relationships: Links tasks to specific components or assemblies Defines which parts are inspected, serviced, or replaced Supports task applicability based on installed parts Enables part-specific maintenance requirements Using Part Number Information: Material Planning - Identify parts needed for upcoming maintenance Procurement - Generate purchase requisitions for required parts Inventory Management - Ensure adequate stock levels Task Applicability - Determine if task applies based on installed parts Configuration Control - Track part number changes and modifications Part number relationships are inherited from the Master Task Card but can be reviewed and verified within the OMP task context. Best Practices: Verify part numbers are current and accurate Maintain alternate part number lists for flexibility Coordinate with supply chain for critical or long-lead items Update part numbers when engineering changes occur Document part number changes in task revision history Effectivity​ The Effectivity section for OMP tasks defines the list of aircraft to which the selected task is applicable. This is more granular than OMP-level effectivity and allows for task-specific applicability rules. Users can change MSN (Manufacturer Serial Number) effectivity to be a serial range using standard format (comma-separated or double-dot notation to indicate a range). Task Effectivity Features: Aircraft-specific task applicability within the OMP Serial number range support for efficient effectivity definition Modification status-based applicability (PRE MOD / POST MOD) Advanced boolean expressions for complex effectivity logic Integration with Technical Publication embodiment status Effectivity Fields: Field Description Aircraft Specific aircraft registration or tail number Serial Number Manufacturer serial number or range Effectivity Type Individual, Range, or Expression Modification Status PRE MOD, POST MOD, or ADVANCED Technical Publication Reference to modification or service bulletin Effectivity Expression Boolean expression for advanced logic Status Active, Inactive, or Pending Serial Number Range Formats: Individual - Single serial number: 12345 Comma-Separated - Multiple individual serial numbers: 12345, 12346, 12350 Range Notation - Continuous range: 12345..12360 (includes all serial numbers from 12345 to 12360) Combined - Mix of individual and ranges: 12345, 12350..12360, 12365 Modification Status Applicability: Modification Status can be used to specify PRE MOD or POST MOD applicability. The task applicability is then determined in relation to whether the selected Technical Publication is embodied against the aircraft or not. PRE MOD - Task applies to aircraft BEFORE the modification is embodied POST MOD - Task applies to aircraft AFTER the modification is embodied ADVANCED - Complex boolean expression determines applicability PRE MOD Example: Task: "Inspect hydraulic pump mounting bracket" Modification Status: PRE MOD Technical Publication: SB-737-29-1234 Applicability: Task applies only to aircraft that have NOT embodied SB-737-29-1234 POST MOD Example: Task: "Inspect modified hydraulic pump mounting bracket" Modification Status: POST MOD Technical Publication: SB-737-29-1234 Applicability: Task applies only to aircraft that HAVE embodied SB-737-29-1234 Advanced Effectivity Expressions: If Modification Status is set to ADVANCED, a boolean expression can be specified which incorporates the following functions: Function Description Example PREMOD Aircraft does not have modification embodied PREMOD("SB-737-29-1234") POSTMOD Aircraft has modification embodied POSTMOD("SB-737-29-1234") MODEL Aircraft model matches specified value MODEL("737-800") ACTYPE Aircraft type matches specified value ACTYPE("737") VARIANT Aircraft variant matches specified value VARIANT("ER") CONFIG Aircraft configuration matches specified value CONFIG("PASSENGER") ROLE Aircraft role matches specified value ROLE("CARGO") STRINGVALUE Custom string attribute matches value STRINGVALUE("WINGLETS", "YES") INTVALUE Custom integer attribute matches value INTVALUE("SEATS", 180) SERIALRANGE Serial number falls within specified range SERIALRANGE("12345..12360") Advanced Expression Examples: Example 1: POST MOD with Model Restriction POSTMOD("SB-737-29-1234") AND MODEL("737-800") Task applies only to 737-800 aircraft that have embodied SB-737-29-1234. Example 2: Serial Range with Configuration SERIALRANGE("12345..12360") AND CONFIG("PASSENGER") Task applies to aircraft with serial numbers 12345 through 12360 that are configured for passenger operations. Example 3: Multiple Modifications POSTMOD("SB-737-29-1234") AND PREMOD("SB-737-29-5678") Task applies to aircraft that have embodied SB-737-29-1234 but have NOT embodied SB-737-29-5678. Example 4: Complex Logic with Multiple Conditions (MODEL("737-800") OR MODEL("737-900")) AND POSTMOD("SB-737-29-1234") AND SERIALRANGE("12345..12360, 12400..12450") Task applies to 737-800 or 737-900 aircraft with specific serial number ranges that have embodied the modification. Example 5: Configuration-Based with String Value CONFIG("CARGO") AND STRINGVALUE("CARGO_DOOR", "INSTALLED") Task applies to cargo-configured aircraft that have a cargo door installed. Example 6: Role and Variant Combination ROLE("MILITARY") AND VARIANT("MARITIME_PATROL") AND INTVALUE("HARDPOINTS", 6) Task applies to military maritime patrol variant aircraft with 6 hardpoints. Advanced effectivity expressions must be carefully tested to ensure they produce the intended results. Incorrect expressions can lead to tasks being applied to wrong aircraft or not applied when needed. Boolean Operators: AND - Both conditions must be true OR - Either condition must be true NOT - Negates the condition Parentheses () - Groups conditions for proper evaluation order Best Practices for Effectivity: Use serial ranges instead of individual entries when possible for efficiency Test advanced expressions thoroughly before activating Document the intent of complex effectivity logic Review effectivity when modifications are embodied Coordinate with engineering for modification-based effectivity Maintain clear records of effectivity changes Verify task applicability after aircraft modifications Effectivity Validation: The system validates effectivity expressions to ensure: Syntax is correct Referenced functions are valid Technical Publications exist in the system Serial number ranges are properly formatted Boolean logic is properly structured

Checks are task cards of type CHECK that are used to group OMP tasks of similar frequencies into larger maintenance events. This grouping is essential for efficient maintenance planning and execution within the Work Package application. Checks provide a structured way to organize multiple tasks that are performed together during scheduled maintenance events. Check Characteristics: Task card with type = CHECK Groups multiple OMP tasks with similar intervals Used for maintenance planning and work package creation Represents major maintenance events (A-Check, C-Check, etc.) Defines check content (list of included tasks) Supports hierarchical check structures Common Check Types: Check Type Typical Interval Description Daily Check 1 Day Daily inspection and servicing Weekly Check 7 Days Weekly inspection tasks A-Check 500-800 FH Light maintenance check B-Check 4-6 Months Intermediate maintenance check C-Check 18-24 Months Heavy maintenance check D-Check 6-10 Years Major overhaul and inspection Phase Check Varies Phased maintenance program segment Check Information: Field Description Check ID Unique identifier for the check Description Detailed description of the check Check Type Category of check (A, B, C, D, Phase, etc.) Interval Frequency at which check is performed Duration Estimated time to complete the check Location Where check is typically performed Check Content List of OMP tasks included in the check Creating a Check: Navigate to the Checks tab on the OMP Main Page Click Add Row or New Check Enter a unique Check ID Provide a descriptive name Select the check type Define the check interval Save the check Check Content: The Check Content section lists all OMP tasks that form part of the check. This defines which maintenance tasks are performed during the check event. Managing Check Content: Select a check from the Checks list Navigate to the Check Content tab Review the list of tasks currently included in the check Add or remove tasks as needed Verify task frequencies align with check interval Save changes Check Content Fields: Field Description Task Card OMP task identifier Description Task description Task Type Type of maintenance task Frequency Task interval Estimated Hours Labor hours for the task Sequence Order in which task is performed Zone Aircraft zone where task is performed Add OMP Tasks to Check: The "Add OMP Tasks to Check" function opens a dialog that allows you to search for OMP tasks in the current OMP and add them as check content. Various criteria can be entered to filter and find appropriate tasks. Search Criteria: Criterion Description Task Frequency Filter by task interval (e.g., 500 FH, 12 MO) Task Type Filter by maintenance task type Trade Filter by required maintenance trade Zone Filter by aircraft zone System Filter by aircraft system (ATA chapter) Keyword Search task descriptions for keywords Effectivity Filter by aircraft applicability Adding Tasks to a Check: Click Add OMP Tasks to Check button Enter search criteria to filter tasks: Specify task frequency range (e.g., 400-600 FH) Select task types (Inspection, Service, etc.) Choose specific trades or zones Enter keywords to search descriptions Review the filtered list of available tasks Select tasks to add to the check (use checkboxes) Click Add Selected to add tasks to check content Verify tasks were added successfully Close the dialog Using frequency-based filtering when adding tasks to checks ensures that all tasks with similar intervals are grouped together for efficient maintenance planning. Frequency-Based Task Grouping: When organizing tasks into checks, consider: Group tasks with similar intervals (±10% tolerance) Include tasks that can be performed simultaneously Consider aircraft downtime and resource availability Balance workload across different checks Coordinate tasks that require similar access or equipment Check Planning Considerations: Task Dependencies - Some tasks must be performed in specific order Resource Requirements - Ensure adequate personnel and equipment Access Requirements - Group tasks requiring similar aircraft access Duration - Balance check duration with operational needs Facility Requirements - Some checks require specific facilities or equipment Best Practices for Check Management: Align check intervals with operational schedules Group tasks logically by system, zone, or trade Minimize aircraft downtime by efficient task grouping Review and update check content regularly Coordinate with maintenance planning for check scheduling Document check structure and rationale Consider seasonal or operational factors in check planning Check Hierarchy: Checks can be organized hierarchically: Major Checks (C-Check, D-Check) contain multiple sub-checks Sub-Checks (Phase 1, Phase 2) break major checks into manageable segments Task Packages group related tasks within sub-checks Hierarchical structure supports phased maintenance programs Integration with Work Packages: Checks are used in the Work Package application to: Generate work packages for scheduled maintenance Organize tasks into logical work groups Estimate resource requirements and duration Track check completion and compliance Support maintenance planning and scheduling Related Documentation: Master Task Cards Application Work Package Application Models Application Part Number Master Technical Records Management Preventive Maintenance Overview Additional Resources: OMP configuration guidelines Effectivity expression syntax reference Check planning best practices Regulatory compliance requirements Maintenance program development procedures
This page gives details on advanced BDI configuration. This involves making direct modifications to the ManageWorkspace custom resource (CR) by an Open Shift administrator.

Two BDI settings can be configured by updating (or patching) the "bdiConfigurations" section of the ManageWorkspace Custom Resource. Setting Description imagePullPolicy Determines when the BDI image will be retrieved from the IBM Entitled Registry. By default the value is: IfNotPresent. This setting is mainly used for internal development purposes. enableRoute: Determines whether an external Route is created, by the BDI entity manager, to the BDI OpenShift service. An external route can be useful for examining the BDI API documentation (Swagger docs) or making BDI API calls from an external system. A valid MAS 'x-access-token' cookie is required for external BDI requests. The default is for the Route to be enabled. Because the "bdiConfigurations" property of the ManageWorkspace custom resource is recorded in an Array it is recommended to update the yaml definition directly in the Open Shift console if modifying any of these additional properties. If an OC patch command is used to update the bdiConfigurations section of the ManageWorkspace Custom Resource then all of the properties in the bdiConfiguration array element must be specified. This is a limitation of the Kubernetes patch command.

The ManageWorkspace custom resource spec.components.acm can be updated to specify BDI container pod templates. For example to override the resources for the BDI Instance "bdi-1" the following yaml is specified: spec: bindings: jdbc: workspace-application components: acm: podTemplates: - containers: - name: bdiservice resources: limits: cpu: 3 memory: 8Gi requests: cpu: 1 memory: 1Gi name: bdi-1 replicas: 1

The BDI pod can be disabled completed by setting the replicas property to zero: spec: bindings: jdbc: workspace-application components: acm: podTemplates: - containers: - name: bdiservice name: bdi-1 replicas: 0
The following podTemplates fields are supported: replicas resources affinity tolerations securityContext nodeSelector topologySpreadConstraints

The Build Data Interpreter (BDI) validates aircraft configuration changes through containerized BDI Pods. The diagram below represents the main interaction points between the BDI pods and the Maximo Manage application and database:

BDI Status Dialog​ Interactive UI for configuration validation: Displays current and alternate configurations Initiates validation via API calls Shows validation results BDI Cron Tasks​ Process Asynchronous jobs generated by the BDI Monitors MAXASYNCJOB queue for submitted jobs Submits jobs for processing using Maximo Business Objext (MBO) logic Update job status to COMPLETE or ERROR despending on result of processing. If BDI Cron Tasks stop running, asynchronous jobs will not be processed and import actions such as automatic work order generation may cease.

Four key tables coordinate BDI workflow: PLUSAANTRAN (Transaction Queue)​ Primary queue for assets awaiting validation: Stores asset identifiers and configuration details Tracks transaction status (pending, processing, completed) Monitored by BDI "Queue Monitor" component within the BDI pod(s) PLUSAANBDISTATUS (Validation Status)​ Stores configuration validation result status on a per asset basis Default status values are: OK, INVALID, ALERT PLUSANBDIMAPPING (Problem Codes)​ List problems related to the current as-maintained asset configuration. 3 letter problem code defines the type of problem Severity defines the effect on overall configuration status Narrative gives a desription of the source of the problem.

Containerized service performing validation logic: Deployment: Kubernetes-based orchestration Multiple pods can be configured for high availability Horizontal scaling based on workload Independent lifecycle from Maximo

The BDI architecture provides scalable, resilient validation of complex aircraft configurations through: Scalability: Horizontal pod scaling for increased volume Resilience: Fault tolerance via multiple pods and database-backed queues Performance: Asynchronous processing prevents user operation blocking Flexibility: Rule-based validation supports diverse aircraft types Compliance: Comprehensive audit trail for regulatory requirements Understanding this architecture is essential for proper sizing, deployment, and maintenance of BDI systems in production environments.

The ACM and Aviation Options parameters, specified within the BDI Instance configuration, are used to alter the functional behaviour of the BDI. Only one option is used and this is determined by which product is installed. The list of options available, and the effect they have on the BDI behaviour, is described in the table below. Those options that are only available in Maximo Aviation are indicated with a "Y" in the "Aviation Only" column. Option Value Description Aviation Only ECP Enables Event Calculation Persistence. The BDI will calculate and save values for the following fields on the PLUSALFEVENT table: P_LEFT, P_DUECOUNT, P_ENDITEMDUECOUNT, CALCDUEDATE, DATEDUECALC. P_LEFT = The number of days remaining until the due date or the number of meter units remaining until the due count. P_DUECOUNT = The due count at which the event (PM) will be due. P_ENDITEMDUECOUNT = The count at which the event (PM) will become due for the top level end item asset record. CALCDUEDATE = The estimated due date at which the event (PM) is due. This is equal to the due date for time based events. For meter based events this will be determined from the units remaining and the meter average of the asset. DUEDATECALC = The date and time when the PLUSALFEVENT record was last updated. N DCR Enables the Due Count Reached feature. When enabled in combination with the ECP option the BDI will "freeze" the PLUSALFEVENT.CALCDUEDATE for meter based events at the point the event became overdue. N MEL Enables MEL (Minimum Essential List) rules validation. A MEL problem is reported when the number of installed and operational items is less than the number required. The MEL is defined on the associated Model record. N MEL-RL MEL problems are reported by Label. Requires MEL option to be enabled. N MEL-RP MEL problems are reported by Position code. Requires MEL option to be enabled. N SRC Enables the evaluation and validation of Systems, Roles, and Capabilities. Roles and Capabilities are defined within the application "Asset/Aircraft Roles and Capabilities". N FLB Enables Flight Log Book validation (e.g. reporting AOG if Aircraft Status = GROUNDED) N OWO Enables monitoring for Orphan Work Orders; A BDI problem code "OWO" is reported when a PM is made INACTIVE and open work orders exist for the PM. N OWJ Enables monitoring for revised Job Plans; A BDI problem code "OWJ" is reported for open work orders where the associated Job Plan was revised post creation of the work order but before its completion. N OWT Enables monitoring for PMs. A BDI problem code "OWT" is reported for each open work order where the PM it was generated from was revised post its creation but before its completion. N TSX Enables persistence of Time Since Repair/Overhaul/Inspection and Life to Date Values. When enabled the BDI will calculate and persist life values in the PLUSAASSETTIMESINCE table for each configuration-managed asset/meter combination: SINCELASTREPAIR SINCELASTOVERHAUL SINCELASTINSPECT, SINCELASTINSPECT2 SINCEINSTALL LIFETODATE N XPM See detalied explanation below N -TRPNR Disables the Part Number Range capability associated with Technical Records. This option is mandatory when using the BDI with ACM. N PME Enables PM Extensions logic. Required when PM Extensions should be considered when evaluating PM Due Date/Counts. N SQP Enables the validation of Serialized Quantity Positions. Determines whether the BDI will report viloation of min/max quantity values when, a build position in a Model, is defined as a mutiple serialized quantity position. N SFT Enables Soft Task validation. When a PM is flagged as a Soft Task (PM.PLUSASOFTTASK=Y) then the BDI Problem Codes associated with PM Due, Warning and Alert intervals are altered to the following. SBA - Soft Task Beyond Alert. SBW = Soft Task Beyond Warning. SBD - Soft Task Beyond Due. The SBD code is treated as an Alert conditionby default. (Compared with INVALID for and overdue non-Soft Task.) N PMR When enabled the BDI will consider the "New Date" value specified on PM Forecast records when determining the PM Due Date. N OMP Enables monitoring for expired OMPs. A BDI probem code "OEX" is raised for active OMP records where the associated Expiry Date has been exceeded. (OMP = Operators Maintenance Plan). Y MPM Enables monitoring and validation of invalid mission flags on FLBs; MPM = Mission Profile-based Maintenance Y W&B Enables Weight and Balance validation. When enabled the BDI will report a "WAB" problem code when the latest Weight and Balance record for an Aircraft is flagged as being outside of the expected variance (as defined in the associated Aircraft Model). Y WOL Enables Whichever Occurs Later / Due on Last Deadline logic. When a Task Card is marked as "Due on Last Deadline?" (PM.PLUSADOLDEADLINE=Y) then it will only be considered overdue when all deadlines are exceeded (considers both Time and Meter Based frequencies/intervals) Y MPC Deprecated. Y SHL Enables Shelf Life logic. Y -UFI This is an Oracle DB Specific option. When specified, it will disable the use and automatic creation of functional indexes on the rowstamp column of tables which the BDI montiors. The BDI uses rowstamp values to monitor for changes within the Maximo database. Maximo on Oracle uses the datatype VARCHAR2 for rowstamp values which can makes comparisons of rowstamp values of different lengths uncertain. By default the BDI will create functional indexes of the form: (cast(rowstamp as number) when used with an Oracle DB. This enables queries which order on the rowstamp column to behave reliably. If this option is disabled the BDI will now perform casts on the rowstamp values but will instead restamp all rowstamp values within a monitored tables when it detects rowstamps of different lengths within the table.
